Chapter 6 of 6

Datadog on top

What you will see

About 20 minutes. In the earlier labs you looked at one incident at a time. Here you use Datadog to watch the whole platform: the VM, Confluent Cloud and AWS. You look at the integrations, at tests that call the shop from outside, at monitors and at cost.

Needs: up to three small layers that only change what Datadog collects: dd-streams, dd-synthetics and dd-rum. The step "Turn on the Datadog layers" turns on the ones you want (skip it if you chose everything at once).

Lab 6.1: Datadog on top of the solution #

Start from the demo home #

Open the demo home.

What the demo home shows

It starts with a "Start here" note, then one group per Chapter: what you are seeing, links to the deeper views already filtered to your stack, and the key charts. Group "6. Datadog on top" holds Synthetics, Confluent consumer lag and the cost per hour. Charts of a layer you have not turned on stay empty. Come back to it after each step below.

Turn on the Datadog layers #

Skip this if you chose everything at once.

Add the ones you want to demo.yaml, for example layers: core,releases,dd-streams,dd-synthetics,dd-rum, then run one command per layer:

Terminal (both paths)
make layer-on L=dd-streams CONFIRM=yes
make layer-on L=dd-synthetics CONFIRM=yes
make layer-on L=dd-rum CONFIRM=yes

Steps 1, 2, 5 and 6 need none of them. Datadog usage runs on your trial; check your trial terms. Skip the steps of a layer you did not turn on.

More about this step

What these layers change. This lab uses three small layers that only change what Datadog collects.

What each Datadog layer creates.

Layer What it creates Used in step
dd-streams A read-only Confluent identity and the Datadog Confluent Cloud integration (consumer lag) 3
dd-synthetics A Synthetics private location on the VM and two tests (an API test every 60 s, a browser test every 300 s) 4
dd-rum A RUM application, and the Online shop is redeployed with its settings 7

Turn on background sales #

With the control panel

In the control panel, press Sales on on the Background sales card and confirm. You should see sales-on succeeded: Background sales are on: 24/min per store; ....

With the terminal

Terminal (both paths)
make sales-on
Why turn sales on here

The earlier labs started with a reset, which turned background sales off so that the numbers were predictable. This lab looks at the platform under steady traffic, so you turn them back on. Within a few minutes the dashboards show live traffic.

1. Read back the stack #

With the control panel

Open the stock dashboard. The Pipeline group shows the six core connectors in stock.connect.task_running by connector, plus restock-procurement and procurement-orders if you turned on the restock layer, all running.

With the terminal

Terminal (both paths)
make status

You should see the six core connectors, plus restock-procurement and procurement-orders if you turned on the restock layer, all RUNNING.

More about this step

With the control panel

The control panel header. The header of the control panel shows the running layers and the canary routing.

With the terminal

What else the output lists. The output lists the VM containers, the current routing, the layers that are on and the status of every connector.

Why not DSM for connectors. This is where you check connectors. DSM shows the data flow, but it does not show connector status.

2. AWS-native online dashboard #

Open the AWS-native online dashboard. It shows Fargate CPU and memory by service and version, ElastiCache memory and CPU, and ALB unhealthy targets, next to inventory-api lookup p95 by version. If you ran Lab 3.1, you can see the CPU peak of release 1.1.0.

3. Confluent Cloud integration #

On the stock dashboard, in the Pipeline group, the chart "Confluent Cloud consumer lag (offsets) by group" comes from the Confluent integration (the dd-streams layer). Consumer lag for stock-projector and connect-sellable-redis should stay near zero, which agrees with the probe.

Spikes are normal

A short spike after a burst of records, like the one in the screenshot, is normal; the lag should fall back to near zero.

4. Synthetics #

Open the synthetic tests of your stack. You should see two synthetic tests that run from aws:eu-central-1 against your ALB: an API test of GET /api/availability/P0042 every 60 s, and a browser test of the product page every 300 s.

Where to find it in the Datadog menu

Open Synthetic Monitoring > Tests and search dd-demo-hybrid.

5. Monitors #

Open the monitors of your stack. You should see the freshness, connector, VM Agent, p95-by-version, restock and AWS-side monitors (16 in our test run). A monitor in "No Data" does not mean everything is fine: the signal is missing.

More about this step

From the Datadog menu, open Monitors > Manage Monitors and search tag:project:dd-demo tag:stack:hybrid.

With the control panel

Then open Events > Explorer and search demo action. Every control-panel action posts demo action: <name> started and then succeeded or failed, for example demo action: canary-10 succeeded. The resulting weights are in a weights: tag. Overlay these events on the p95-by-version graph to see exactly when a release change took effect.

With the terminal

Then open Events > Explorer and search demo config. You should see the settings you saved in the panel in Labs 5.1 and 5.2. The make commands post no events, so your routing changes from the terminal do not appear here.

6. Cost #

Open the account-cost dashboard: link and set stack to hybrid.

Burn now (estimate) is the cost per hour right now. Spent this month, cumulative shows the month-to-date bill per vendor and the total, and Confluent credit left shows what remains of the $400 trial credit.

More about this step

Where the numbers come from, and when the billed cost arrives. The cost-meter service estimates the hourly cost of the AWS pieces from list prices and reads Confluent usage. The billed AWS cost arrives later: AWS writes it to the Cost and Usage Report, and Datadog Cloud Cost Management reads it from there, typically 48 to 72 hours after the first complete report.

Why the fix does not change the price of a task. Fargate bills each task by its vCPU and memory size, so the cost estimate follows the task size set in service_sizing (terraform/aws/variables.tf). All three releases use the same size (0.5 vCPU / 1 GB). The fix therefore does not change the hourly price of a task. It changes how much traffic one task can handle (see the CPU comparison in Lab 4.1).

7. Check RUM on your run #

RUM should record your browser sessions. Check that it works on your run: open http://<alb-dns-name>/config in your browser.

Or ask it from the terminal, and the Datadog menu path
Terminal (both paths)
curl -s http://<alb-dns-name>/config

In the Datadog menu, the sessions are under Digital Experience > RUM > Sessions.

You should see a rum block with an application ID and a client token. The client token is meant to be public. Browse the shop for a minute, then open the RUM sessions of the application dd-demo-hybrid-shop. If a session appears, RUM works on your run.

Checkpoint #

  • Every connector is running, six or eight with the restock layer. Control panel: the Pipeline group of the stock dashboard shows them all running · Terminal: make status shows every connector RUNNING (step 1).
  • If dd-synthetics is on: both Synthetics tests have recent passing results (step 4).
  • The cost dashboard shows a current USD-per-hour value for hybrid (step 6).

Summary

Across the labs, APM found the slow request, freshness and DSM showed that the data path was fine, version tags checked the canary, and the integrations and monitors gave you the view of the whole platform.

Switch to the terminal path?

Pick one path and use it from start to finish. The control panel and the terminal each remember their own last routing for Rollback, so mixing them in one run can roll back to the wrong state. Switch only if you are starting a lab from a reset.
